summary.text: Factoring the characteristic polynomial and setting \(w=-1+\sqrt{-15}\), with \(w^2+2w+16=0\), gives the closed form \(a(k)=2\cdot8^k-2(-8)^k+2^k\operatorname{Re}(w^{k+1})\), as it matches the initial values and recurrence. Writing \(w^{n+1}=x+y\sqrt{-15}\), the norm identity \(x^2+15y^2=16^{n+1}\) and \(\operatorname{Re}((w^{n+1})^2)=x^2-15y^2\) simplify the odd-indexed term to \((2^{n+1}x)^2\).

full_proof.text:
Let \((a_n)_{n\ge 0}\) be the integer sequence defined by
\[
a_0=-1,\qquad a_1=4,\qquad a_2=176,\qquad a_3=3136,
\]
and, for every \(n\ge 0\),
\[
a_{n+4}=-4a_{n+3}+256a_{n+1}+4096a_n.
\]
We prove that \(a_{2n+1}\) is a square for every \(n\ge 0\), and in fact exhibit a square root.

Work in the quadratic ring
\[
R=\mathbb Z[\sqrt{-15}].
\]
Thus every element of \(R\) is written as \(x+y\sqrt{-15}\), with \(x,y\in\mathbb Z\), and multiplication uses \((\sqrt{-15})^2=-15\). For
\[
z=x+y\sqrt{-15},
\]
write
\[
\operatorname{Re}(z)=x,
\qquad
\overline z=x-y\sqrt{-15},
\qquad
N(z)=z\overline z=x^2+15y^2.
\]
The norm is multiplicative, since
\[
N(uv)=uv\,\overline{uv}=uv\,\overline u\,\overline v
      =(u\overline u)(v\overline v)=N(u)N(v).
\]

Set
\[
w=-1+\sqrt{-15}.
\]
A direct calculation gives
\[
w^2=(-1+\sqrt{-15})^2=-14-2\sqrt{-15}=-2w-16,
\]
so
\[
w^2+2w+16=0.
\]
Also
\[
N(w)=(-1)^2+15\cdot 1^2=16.
\]
By multiplicativity of the norm, for every \(k\ge 0\),
\[
N(w^k)=N(w)^k=16^k. \tag{1}
\]

We next establish a closed form for the given fourth-order recurrence. Define
\[
f_n=2\cdot 8^n-2\cdot(-8)^n+2^n\operatorname{Re}(w^{n+1}). \tag{2}
\]
We claim that \(f_n=a_n\) for every \(n\).

First, the characteristic polynomial associated with the recurrence is
\[
P(X)=X^4+4X^3-256X-4096.
\]
It factors as
\[
P(X)=(X-8)(X+8)(X^2+4X+64), \tag{3}
\]
because
\[
(X^2-64)(X^2+4X+64)=X^4+4X^3-256X-4096.
\]
Consequently, the sequences \(8^n\) and \((-8)^n\) both obey
\[
u_{n+4}=-4u_{n+3}+256u_{n+1}+4096u_n. \tag{4}
\]

The remaining term in (2) obeys the same recurrence. Indeed, put \(q=2w\). From \(w^2+2w+16=0\),
\[
q^2+4q+64=4(w^2+2w+16)=0.
\]
Hence (3) gives \(P(q)=0\). Multiplying this identity by \(wq^n\) yields
\[
wq^{n+4}+4wq^{n+3}-256wq^{n+1}-4096wq^n=0.
\]
Taking real parts and using
\[
wq^n=w(2w)^n=2^n w^{n+1},
\]
we find that
\[
g_n:=2^n\operatorname{Re}(w^{n+1})
\]
also satisfies (4). Therefore the linear combination \(f_n=2\cdot8^n-2\cdot(-8)^n+g_n\) satisfies the required fourth-order recurrence.

It remains to check its first four values. We have
\[
\operatorname{Re}(w)=-1.
\]
Using \(w=-1+\sqrt{-15}\), one computes
\[
w^2=-14-2\sqrt{-15},
\]
\[
w^3=(-14-2\sqrt{-15})(-1+\sqrt{-15})
    =44-12\sqrt{-15},
\]
and
\[
w^4=(44-12\sqrt{-15})(-1+\sqrt{-15})
    =136+56\sqrt{-15}.
\]
Thus
\[
\begin{aligned}
f_0
 &=2-2+\operatorname{Re}(w)=-1,\\
f_1
 &=2\cdot8-2\cdot(-8)+2\operatorname{Re}(w^2)
   =16+16-28=4,\\
f_2
 &=2\cdot64-2\cdot64+4\operatorname{Re}(w^3)
   =4\cdot44=176,\\
f_3
 &=2\cdot512-2\cdot(-512)+8\operatorname{Re}(w^4)
   =1024+1024+8\cdot136
   =3136.
\end{aligned}
\]
So \(f_0,f_1,f_2,f_3\) agree with \(a_0,a_1,a_2,a_3\). Since both sequences satisfy the same recurrence, they agree everywhere: formally, an induction on \(n\) shows that if equality is known up through index \(n+3\), then the recurrence gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
a_{n+4}
 &=-4a_{n+3}+256a_{n+1}+4096a_n\\
 &=-4f_{n+3}+256f_{n+1}+4096f_n
 =f_{n+4}.
\end{aligned}
\]
We have therefore proved the closed form
\[
a_n=2\cdot 8^n-2\cdot(-8)^n+2^n\operatorname{Re}(w^{n+1}) \tag{5}
\]
for all \(n\ge 0\).

Now fix a nonnegative integer \(n\), and write
\[
z=w^{n+1}=x+y\sqrt{-15}
\]
with \(x,y\in\mathbb Z\). By (1),
\[
x^2+15y^2=N(z)=N(w^{n+1})=16^{n+1}. \tag{6}
\]
Furthermore,
\[
w^{2n+2}=z^2=(x+y\sqrt{-15})^2
              =(x^2-15y^2)+2xy\sqrt{-15},
\]
so
\[
\operatorname{Re}(w^{2n+2})=x^2-15y^2. \tag{7}
\]

Apply (5) at the odd index \(2n+1\). Since \((-8)^{2n+1}=-8^{2n+1}\), we obtain
\[
\begin{aligned}
a_{2n+1}
 &=2\cdot8^{2n+1}-2\cdot(-8)^{2n+1}
   +2^{2n+1}\operatorname{Re}(w^{2n+2})\\
 &=4\cdot8^{2n+1}
   +2^{2n+1}(x^2-15y^2). \tag{8}
\end{aligned}
\]
The first term in (8) can be rewritten using (6). Indeed,
\[
4\cdot8^{2n+1}
 =2^2(2^3)^{2n+1}
 =2^{6n+5},
\]
while
\[
2^{2n+1}16^{n+1}
 =2^{2n+1}(2^4)^{n+1}
 =2^{6n+5}.
\]
Therefore
\[
4\cdot8^{2n+1}
 =2^{2n+1}16^{n+1}
 =2^{2n+1}(x^2+15y^2). \tag{9}
\]
Substituting (9) into (8) gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
a_{2n+1}
 &=2^{2n+1}(x^2+15y^2)
   +2^{2n+1}(x^2-15y^2)\\
 &=2^{2n+1}(2x^2)\\
 &=2^{2n+2}x^2\\
 &=\bigl(2^{n+1}x\bigr)^2.
\end{aligned}
\]
Since \(x=\operatorname{Re}(w^{n+1})\) is an integer, this explicitly exhibits an integer square root:
\[
\boxed{
a_{2n+1}=\left(2^{n+1}\operatorname{Re}\bigl((-1+\sqrt{-15})^{n+1}\bigr)\right)^2.
}
\]
Thus \(a(2n+1)\) is a perfect square for every nonnegative integer \(n\), as claimed.
